item.description:
9:00 - 10:00: Elijah Sheridan (Cornell), "Advances in Calabi-Yau Geometry for String Phenomenology" Abstract: String phenomenology routinely reduces to problems in Calabi-Yau (CY) geometry. This motivates both inquiry into the general structure of the set of CY varieties - constraining the space of UV-complete theories - and development of efficient methods for the explicit computations crucial for building the IR EFT of any fixed compactification. In this direction, I will present progress in two areas of CY geometry.
10:15 - 11:15: Anthony Ashmore (Skidmore), "Supersymmetric deformations, RG flows and their supergravity duals" Abstract: It is a long-standing problem to find the explicit string backgrounds dual to generic N=1 deformations of N=4 super Yang-Mills. We approach this problem using generalised geometry, where supersymmetric AdS backgrounds are described by a pair of geometric structures satisfying algebraic and differential conditions.

"The Great Silence" ["Il grande silenzio"] (Sergio Corbucci, 1968, 105 min, Italy, Italian w/ subtitles, Color, DCP)
On an unforgiving, snow-swept frontier, a group of bloodthirsty bounty hunters, led by the vicious Loco (Klaus Kinski) prey on a band of persecuted outlaws who have taken to the hills. Only a mute gunslinger named Silence (Jean-Louis Trintignant) stands between the innocent refugees and the corrupt bounty hunters. But, in this harsh, brutal world, the lines between right and wrong are not always clear, and good does not always triumph. Featuring superb photography and a haunting score from maestro Ennio Morricone, director Sergio Corbucci's bleak, brilliant and violent vision of an immoral, honorless West is widely considered to be among the best and most influential Westerns ever made.

item.description: Globally, a large fraction of the disease burden is attributed to environmental contaminants, particularly enteric pathogens, which are transmitted via multiple pathways, including water, food, soil, and fomites. Further, microbial contaminants are garnering more public health attention at the global scale due to the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Prioritization of strategies to interrupt the transmission of these microbial contaminants can be informed by environmental monitoring and exposure assessments to determine health risks associated with different behaviors and practices. This talk will present insight from multiple modeling and field investigations seeking to understand transmission dynamics of gastrointestinal pathogens in a variety of settings. Strategies for ensuring environmental monitoring data and risk assessments can inform public health action will be discussed. item.title: Embodied Neuromechanics or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love NeuroAI — Mon Nov 9, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Behavior is the ultimate output of the nervous system, but it has long resisted precise measurement. My lab develops AI tools, including SLEAP, that extract detailed body kinematics from video at scale, turning behavior into quantitative data on par with neural recordings and connectomes. We then use these measurements to build embodied neuromechanical models: artificial neural networks that control physically simulated animal bodies, linking neural circuits, biomechanics, and behavior in a single framework. Because these models are generative, they can simulate perturbations and produce mechanistic hypotheses that can be tested directly at the bench, creating a feedback loop between AI and experimental neuroscience.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Anxious Homes: Inflexible Demand and China's Housing Market — Mon Nov 9, 1:30 PM — Friedl 225
item.description:
Drawing on fieldwork conducted in a gangxu development at the urban periphery of east Nanjing from 2013 to 2015, this talk argues that the concept of "inflexible demand" works as an empty signifier bridging divergent value-making projects that are constitutive of China's housing market. It argues that gangxu is a hegemonic concept through which people contest inclusion and exclusion in relation to the city in contemporary China. The talk is developed from a new book titled "Anxious Homes: Inflexible Demand and China's Housing Market."
About the speaker: Mengqi Wang is an Assistant Professor of Anthropology at Duke Kunshan University (DKU). Her research focus is the intersection among economic anthropology, urban studies, and critical infrastructure studies. She is especially interested in how the home-as an object of attachment, a condition of social reproduction, and a residential property-mediate capital accumulation and urban governance in contemporary China. item.title: On Reproductive Liberty — Mon Nov 9, 5:00 PM — East Duke Parlors
item.description:
This talk interrogates how slavery animates the psychic counters of abortion concerns. From the use of the Civil War as a metaphor for battles over personhood by abortion legal scholars such as Mary Ziegler to the constitutional originalism espoused by Justice Samuel Alito's reading of the fourteenth amendment in Dobbs, slavery occupies a foundational psychic landscape with the rhetorical strategies of abortion battles. To trace this emergence, this talk returns to nineteenth century medical jurisprudence to consider how the concept of portio viscerum matris situates gestation as the dividing line between the status of life and the conditions of property.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Primer to Causal Inference Workshop — Mon Nov 9, 5:00 PM — Bostock Library
item.description:
As ice cream consumption increases, so do shark attacks, but does eating ice cream really cause shark attacks? This example shows how two things can be related without one causing the other. Yet, in research, figuring out whether we can make a causal claim about the relationship between two variables isn't always so simple. This workshop introduces the basics of causal inference and helps you think more carefully about the claims you make as a researcher.
By the end of the workshop, you'll have a better understanding of how to: ~Identify what's needed to establish causality. ~Explore simple experimental and quasi-experimental approaches to studying cause and effect. ~Develop your own causal research questions.
If you want to move beyond identifying relationships and start exploring cause and effect, join us for this workshop.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Fri Feb 5 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.
